stemMd: Two enzymes have the same amino-acid composition but different amino-acid sequences. Which conclusion is justified?

options.label: A
options.textMd: They must contain different kinds of peptide bond.

options.label: B
options.textMd: They must have identical primary structures.

options.label: C
options.textMd: They must have identical active sites.

options.label: D
options.textMd: They may fold differently and catalyse different reactions.

explanationMd: Primary structure specifies residue order, not merely the number of each amino acid. That order influences folding and the chemical environment of an active site. Different sequences can therefore produce different shapes and catalytic activities, even when their overall compositions match. The cautious word “may” matters: different sequences need not always produce different functions.

distractorRationale.c: Composition does not determine the order of residues or the resulting fold.
distractorRationale.a: Both proteins use the same class of peptide linkage.
distractorRationale.b: Primary structure is the sequence, which the premise says differs.
distractorRationale.e: Sequence differences do not imply insolubility or inactivity in water.
